title: Review 4: Sizing cost, planning and feasibility

questions.q: A loom plan shows
options: The floor layout of the shed
Which quality runs on how many looms and when each order will finish
questions.explain: It turns booked orders into daily production, days needed and finish dates.

questions.q: A changeover on a loom means
options: Re-beaming the loom from one quality to another
questions.explain: The loom stops while the new beam is gaited, which costs a day or more of production.

questions.q: In set size planning, a “set” is
options: One full creel of cones warped onto the beams needed for one sizing run
The reed and healds of one loom
questions.explain: The cones on the creel decide how long the warper’s beams, and so the set, can be.

questions.q: The trend line in the sizing-cost lecture is used to
options: Forecast the sizing cost of a count not yet run
questions.explain: A line or curve fitted to past costs lets the planner estimate the cost for a new count.

questions.q: UCM in the feasibility lectures stands for
questions.explain: Selling price per metre minus all variable costs per metre.

questions.q: “Ramp-up” in Planning IV means
options: Looms coming on to the order one by one over several days
questions.explain: Production starts small and grows as looms are released to the order.

questions.q: A positive “late” figure in the loom plan is a warning that the order will miss its vessel.
questions.explain: Negative means days in hand; positive means the goods reach port after the dispatch deadline.

questions.q: Yarn working is the calculation of
options: Daily warp and weft yarn needed by the looms on each quality
The price of yarn in the market
questions.explain: Pounds per yard × production × looms gives the bags needed per day.

questions.q: A feasibility study of a weaving plant compares
options: The profit the plant can earn with the investment it needs
questions.explain: Contribution less fixed costs and depreciation, as a return on the money invested.

questions.q: In the feasibility lecture, the conservative, normal and aggressive scenarios differ in the mix of local and export sales.
questions.explain: Local sale leaves a small contribution per metre and export a much larger one; the scenarios mix them differently.

quizzes.title: Linking the ideas
quizzes.intro: Cause and effect in planning and feasibility.

questions.q: Sizing cost per kilogram rises with finer counts mainly because
options: A kilogram of finer yarn has more length and surface to coat, and runs slower
questions.explain: More metres per kilogram mean more surface, more add-on and more machine time per kilogram.

questions.q: An order is running late. Which action does NOT bring the finish date forward?
questions.explain: More picks per inch would slow production. The other three raise the daily output.

questions.q: Days needed for an order equal
options: Quantity ÷ daily production of the looms assigned
questions.explain: Divide what must be made by what the assigned looms make in a day.

questions.q: Stock on a shipment day is
options: Looms × rate on that day only
Cumulative production to that day minus earlier shipments
questions.explain: The ledger adds each day’s production and subtracts what has already been shipped.

questions.q: The length of yarn on one cone is
questions.explain: Weight × yards per pound, less the yarn lost as wastage.

questions.q: If each loom gets a longer sized beam, the number of sets needed for the same looms
questions.explain: More warp length must come from cones of fixed length, so the creel has to be filled more often.

questions.q: A cut of Rs 1 in the selling price per metre reduces the monthly contribution of a plant by
options: Rs 1 × metres produced in the month
questions.explain: Every metre sold earns one rupee less.

questions.q: Idle looms shown in the changeover plan are capacity that can be offered for new bookings.
questions.explain: The gap between looms running and looms in the shed is what marketing can still sell.

questions.q: Return on investment in the feasibility sheet is
questions.explain: It is the yearly profit as a percentage of the money put into the plant.

questions.q: Depreciation is ignored in the feasibility of a new plant because it is not paid in cash.
questions.explain: The looms wear out and must be paid for out of profits, so depreciation is deducted before the return is judged.

quizzes.title: Mixed calculations
quizzes.intro: Planning arithmetic: days, stock, cones and returns.

questions.q: Sizing cost follows the trend: cost per kg = 3.50 + 0.15 × Ne. What cost does it forecast for a Ne 40 warp, in rupees to two decimals?
An order of 90,000 m is put on 12 looms, each making 300 m a day. How many days does it take?
Weaving finishes on day 43. Packing takes 2 days and transport to Karachi 4 days. On what day do the goods reach Karachi?
The vessel sails on day 56 and goods must be in Karachi 4 days before. Goods arrive on day 49. How many days are in hand?
questions.explain: Deadline = day 52; 52 − 49 = 3 days in hand.

questions.q: Six looms each use 0.68 bags of warp a day. How many bags of warp do they use in 12 days, to one decimal?

Looms come on to an order one every two days, starting with one loom on day 1 (so 1 loom on days 1–2, 2 looms on days 3–4, and so on). Each loom makes 200 m a day. How much is produced in the first 6 days?
A cone of 4.17 lb of Ne 20 loses 2% as wastage. What length does it supply, to the nearest yard?
A quality needs 139,000 yards of warper’s-beam length and each cone supplies 68,655 yards. How many sets is that, to two decimals?
questions.explain: 139,000 ÷ 68,655 = 2.02 sets, which is run as 2.

questions.q: Two sets are warped with 807 ends per beam. With 24 cones to a bag, how many bags of yarn must be issued, to the nearest bag?
questions.explain: 807 cones per creel × 2 sets ÷ 24 = 67 bags.

questions.q: A fabric sells at Rs 53 a metre and its variable cost is Rs 48.78. A loom makes 430 m a day. What is the contribution per loom per day, to the nearest rupee?

quizzes.title: Case study
quizzes.intro: Is the 40-loom shed worth building? Work it through from one metre to the yearly return.

questions.q: What is the unit contribution margin per metre?
questions.explain: 60 − 42 − 4 = Rs 14 per metre.

questions.q: What is the contribution per loom per day?
How many metres does the shed produce in a month?
What is the contribution of the shed per month?
What is the depreciation per month?
What is the profit per month after fixed costs and depreciation?
What is the yearly return on the investment, in percent to one decimal?
How many metres a month must be sold to break even (covering fixed costs and depreciation), to the nearest metre?
questions.explain: 3,900,000 ÷ 14 = 278,571 metres, about 52% of capacity.

questions.q: If the selling price falls by Rs 2 a metre, by how much does the monthly profit fall?

quizzes.case: A new shed of 40 looms will weave one quality. Each loom makes 450 metres a day. The selling price is Rs 60 a metre; yarn costs Rs 42 a metre and sizing, packing and commission Rs 4 a metre. Monthly fixed costs (salaries, stores, overheads and administration) are Rs 2,400,000. The investment is Rs 180 million, depreciated in equal amounts over 10 years. Take a month as 30 days.

quizzes.title: Group challenge
quizzes.intro: Planning problems with more than one step.

questions.q: An order of 120,000 yards is woven on 8 looms at 500 rpm, 80% efficiency and 60 picks per inch, with 2% B-grade. How many days does it take, to one decimal?

Six looms start an order on day 1, each making 230 m a day. A shipment of 40,000 m is booked for day 40, loaded from stock made up to the end of day 39. How many metres are left in stock after loading?
A quality has 8,064 ends and the creel holds 840 cones. Beams are rounded up to an even number. How many ends go on each beam, to the nearest whole number?
Ten warper’s beams must each carry 13,900 yards. A cone supplies 68,655 yards. How many times must the creel be filled (sets), to two decimals?
questions.explain: Total beam length 139,000 yd ÷ 68,655 = 2.02; each cone feeds one end on beam after beam.

questions.q: A plant earns a contribution of Rs 2,450,000 a month on local sales and Rs 7,080,000 on export. What is the monthly contribution of a 50/50 mix?
A plant costs Rs 216 million. Monthly contribution is Rs 4,765,000, fixed costs Rs 1,200,000 and depreciation is over 12 years. What is the yearly return in percent, to one decimal?
Sizing costs for five counts lie on a curve that bends upward. A straight-line forecast for a much finer count will probably be
questions.explain: A straight line cannot follow the rising curve, so beyond the data it underestimates. The quadratic fit follows it better.

questions.q: The 98 inch quality has only about 18,500 m in hand after its second shipment, while the 68 inch quality has 36,000 m. If looms are released late, which shipment is at risk first?
questions.explain: The thinner margin is the one a delay will wipe out first.

questions.q: If a set works out at 2.03, running 2 sets simply makes each beam a little shorter than planned.
questions.explain: The small shortfall is spread over all the beams instead of filling the creel a third time.

questions.q: A shed has 20 looms. On day 10 the plan shows 6 looms on quality A, 6 on B and 8 on C. A new order needing 4 looms from day 10 can be
options: Accepted only after one of the running lots finishes
Accepted by adding picks per inch
Accepted if the reed is changed
questions.explain: All 20 looms are busy on day 10; the total running can never exceed the looms in the shed.
